overview: Srivijaya, a Malay kingdom based at Palembang on Sumatra from the seventh century, controlled the Strait of Malacca and the trade between India and China. Its rulers were patrons of Buddhism, and Old Malay, the language of its inscriptions, became the lingua franca of the archipelago.

items.text: The kingdom taxed ships passing the strait and made its ports the entrepot of the sea route between India and China.
Camphor, resins, gold, tin and spices went out; Chinese and Indian goods came in.
Missions to the Tang and Song courts kept the China trade open, and Arab writers knew the maharaja of Zabaj as lord of the islands.
The Chinese monk Yijing stopped at Srivijaya in 671 and found more than a thousand monks; he advised pilgrims to study Sanskrit there before going on to India.
The Kedukan Bukit inscription of 683, in Old Malay, is the oldest dated text in the language.
Mahayana Buddhism had royal patronage; the scholar Atisha studied at Srivijaya for twelve years before carrying its teaching to Tibet.
Malay spread as the trading language of the region and is the root of modern Malay and Indonesian.
The pattern of a port kingdom ruling the strait passed to Malacca.

fall.text: The Cholas sacked the ports in 1025, Malayu at Jambi took the lead, and Javanese Singhasari and Majapahit pressed on Sumatra; Majapahit's attack on Palembang in 1377 ended the old kingdom.
